'''Darren Paul Flutie'''  (born November 18, 1966) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Boston College Eagles football|Boston College Eagles]]. After a brief stint in the NFL, Flutie played in the CFL for the [[BC Lions]], [[Edmonton Eskimos]], and [[Hamilton Tiger-Cats]]. He is the CFL's [[List of Canadian Football League records (individual)#Receiving|fifth all-time leader in catches]], behind [[Nik Lewis]], [[Geroy Simon]], [[Ben Cahoon]], and [[Terry Vaughn]].

He played [[college football]] for the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Arizona State Sun Devils]], and was selected by the Cowboys in the second round of the [[1992 NFL draft]] with the 37th overall pick. He finished his career with six [[Pro Bowl]] selections, including three first-team All-Pro selections, and won three [[Super Bowl|Super Bowls]].

<!-- Please see talk page consensus pertaining to mentioning his criminal status in the opening sentence. -->'''Darren Mallory Sharper''' (born November 3, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[safety (American football position)|safety]] and convicted rapist who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 14 seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[William & Mary Tribe football|William & Mary Tribe]] and was selected in the second round of the [[1997 NFL draft]] by the [[Green Bay Packers]], where he spent eight seasons. Sharper played his next four seasons with the [[Minnesota Vikings]] and his final two with the [[New Orleans Saints]].

Recognized as one of the league's top defensive backs during his career, Sharper was a five-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection and a two-time first-team [[All-Pro]], along with being named to the second-team of the [[National Football League 2000s All-Decade Team|2000s All-Decade Team]]. He ranks sixth in interceptions and is tied with [[Charles Woodson]] and [[Rod Woodson]] for the most defensive touchdowns.

Following Sharper's 2010 retirement, allegations surfaced that he drugged and raped several women across various states, leading to him being charged in 2014. Sharper pled guilty to the rape and drug-related charges and was sentenced in 2016 to 20 years in prison. As a result of his guilty plea, he was removed from the [[College of William & Mary]]  Athletics Hall of Fame. Although the conviction did not disqualify his [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] eligibility, Sharper never progressed beyond nomination in the voting process.<ref>{{cite news |first=Mather |last=Victor |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/21/sports/football/darren-sharper-pro-football-hall-of-fame.html |title=How Was a Serial Rapist Nominated to the Pro Football Hall of Fame? |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 20, 2016 |access-date=May 1, 2023}}</ref>

'''Darren Deon McFadden''' (born August 27, 1987) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 10 seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[Arkansas Razorbacks football|Arkansas Razorbacks]] and was selected by the [[Oakland Raiders]] in the first round with the fourth overall pick of the [[2008 NFL draft]]. McFadden also played three seasons for the [[Dallas Cowboys]].

At Arkansas, McFadden had a decorated career, twice finishing as a finalist for the [[Heisman Trophy]] and as a consensus member of the [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] team. He was highly touted coming out of school, and was picked fourth overall by the Raiders. McFadden struggled with consistency through his professional career, only rushing for over 1,000 yards twice and never started all 16 games of a season. McFadden retired midway through the 2017 NFL season, and was voted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2019.

'''Darren Comeaux''' (born April 15, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for the [[Denver Broncos]] (1982–86), [[San Francisco 49ers]] (1987) and [[Seattle Seahawks]] (1988–91) of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Arizona State Sun Devils]].

He helped the Broncos win the 1984 [[AFC West|AFC West Division]] and the 1986 [[American Football Conference Championship Game|AFC Championship]], the 49ers win the 1987 [[NFC West|NFC West Division]] and the Seahawks the 1988 AFC West Division.

Darren Comeaux grew up in California playing basketball and running track didn't start playing football until he was in high school. Once out of high school Darren attended [[San Diego Mesa College|San Diego Mesa Community College]] and eventually went to [[Arizona State University]]. Darren was undersized while in college weighing only 195 pounds, this being the main reason scouts weren't looking at him. He bulked up to 240 pounds and ended up on the Denver Broncos in 1982. While on the Broncos, he helped his team get to [[Super Bowl XXI]] but they would lose to the Giants 39–20. When he was on the San Francisco 49ers he suffered a knee injury which left him on injury reserve. While on injury reserve he was taken by the Seattle Seahawks in 1988 and replaced Brian Bosworth when he had a shoulder injury. Darren led the Seahawks in tackles consecutively and retired after spending 10 years in the league. He finished his NFL career in 1991, in 10 seasons he had over 100 tackles, 3½ sacks, 3 interceptions and he even returned 1 kickoff.
